## Proof

Define the entire function
$$g(z) = f''(z) + f(z).$$
Since $f$ is entire, so are $f''$ and $g$.

The hypothesis gives $g(1/n) = 0$ for every positive integer $n$. The sequence $\{1/n\}_{n\ge 1}$ consists of distinct nonzero points converging to $0$, and $0$ lies in the domain of $g$ (which is all of $\mathbb{C}$). By the identity theorem for holomorphic functions, an entire function whose zeros accumulate at a point of its domain must vanish identically. Hence
$$g(z) \equiv 0, \quad\text{i.e.,}\quad f''(z) + f(z) = 0 \quad \text{for all } z\in\mathbb{C}.$$

This is the linear ODE $f'' = -f$ with constant coefficients. Its general solution is
$$f(z) = A\cos z + B\sin z,$$
where $A, B$ are arbitrary complex constants. These functions are entire, and they satisfy $f''+f = -A\cos z - B\sin z + A\cos z + B\sin z = 0$ identically, so in particular the condition holds at $z = 1/n$ for every $n$.

Conversely, every entire solution of $f''+f=0$ is of this form (the characteristic equation $r^2+1=0$ gives $r=\pm i$, and the two-dimensional solution space over $\mathbb{C}$ is spanned by $\cos z$ and $\sin z$).

Therefore the entire functions satisfying the given condition are exactly
$$\boxed{f(z) = A\cos z + B\sin z,\qquad A,B\in\mathbb{C}.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
